title: Vision and Athletics
sub: How Your Eyes Affect Performance · Grades 5–8 · PE · 25 minutes
objective: Students will understand how visual perception directly affects athletic performance, experience how depth perception and peripheral vision impact sports skills, and practice drills that improve hand-eye coordination and visual reaction time.
materials: Tennis balls or similar soft balls (one per pair)
Eye patches or paper/tape to cover one eye (optional)
Different colored balls or objects (for color recognition drill)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit:** The stereoscope shows how two slightly different images create depth perception.

steps.title: The one-eye challenge
script: **Quick demonstration:** Ask for a volunteer. Have them stand 10 feet away and toss them a ball to catch—first with both eyes open (easy catch), then with one eye covered (much harder).

*“Why was that so much harder with one eye? Your two eyes work together to create depth perception—the ability to judge how far away things are. When you lose one eye’s input, catching becomes really difficult because you can’t tell exactly where the ball is in space. Today we’re going to explore how your vision affects your athletic performance!”*

screen.question: Why was that so much harder with one eye?

steps.purpose: Feel depth perception at work before naming it.

steps.title: Three visual skills in sports
script: **Depth perception:** Both eyes judge distance; **Critical for:** catching, hitting, shooting; A 90 mph baseball gives you <0.5 sec to judge position
**Peripheral vision:** “Corner of your eye” vision; **Critical for:** soccer, basketball, hockey; Athletes train to notice more at the edges
**Reaction time:** Speed of visual processing; **Critical for:** goalkeeping, batting; Pros vs amateurs = milliseconds
*“Professional athletes train these visual skills just like they train their muscles. Let’s try some of their drills!”*

cells: A 90 mph baseball gives you <0.5 sec to judge position
Athletes train to notice more at the edges

steps.purpose: Name the three skills the stations will train.
students: Let’s try some of their drills!

steps.title: Station 1: Depth perception challenge
script: Set up three stations. Students rotate through each (4–5 minutes per station).
**Setup:** Partners 10–15 feet apart. Toss ball with both eyes (count catches out of 5), then one eye covered (repeat). Switch roles.
**Discussion:** *“How much harder with one eye? This is why depth perception matters!”*

screen.question: How much harder with one eye?

steps.purpose: Students rotate to this station and run the drill in pairs.
students: Toss ball with both eyes (count catches out of 5), then one eye covered (repeat).

steps.title: Station 2: Peripheral vision drill
script: Set up three stations. Students rotate through each (4–5 minutes per station).

**Setup:** Student faces forward, partner to the side. Partner slowly moves ball from behind toward field of vision. Student says “NOW” when they first see it (without moving eyes). Repeat on other side, switch.
**Challenge:** Can you detect the ball earlier with practice?

screen.question: Can you detect the ball earlier with practice?

steps.purpose: Students rotate to this station and run the drill in pairs.
students: Student faces forward, partner to the side.
Partner slowly moves ball from behind toward field of vision.

steps.title: Station 3: Reaction time challenge
script: Set up three stations. Students rotate through each (4–5 minutes per station).

**Setup:** Partners face each other with colored objects. Partner A holds up color; Partner B calls color AND performs action (Red = clap, Blue = jump, Yellow = touch ground). Count correct out of 10, switch.

steps.title: Connect to the exhibition
script: *“Your brain constantly processes visual info and makes predictions—sometimes wrong (illusions), sometimes right (catching). The more you train your visual system, the better your predictions become.”*
